newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices firm on Iran-Germany diplomatic row.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices firm on Iran-Germany diplomatic row.

text.p: World oil prices firmed on Friday, supported by a political row between Iran and Germany and below-normal temperatures in the United States, the world's leading crude oil importer.
World benchmark Brent blend May futures was trading 22 cents a barrel higher at $18.15 at 1151 GMT on London's International Petroleum Exchange (IPE).
New York's West Texas Intermediate (WTI) May futures contracts were trading six cents higher at $19.63 a barrel on the ACCESS after-hours electronic trading system.
"There's every sign that the market is moving higher over the next day or so," one IPE broker said.

Brokers said the market firmed on news of a row between Bonn and Tehran over the 1992 killing of Kurdish exiles in Berlin and reports that a new cold spell would affect the United States up to early next week.
"Technically, WTI and crude are doing well...News-wise people are watching the Germany-Iran diplomatic standoff and the cold weather in the United States," the broker said.

Brokers said the oil market would be watching developments in the row between Germany and Iran, which erupted after a German court ruling on Thursday implicated Tehran in the killing of four Kurdish dissidents in a Berlin restaurant.

Germany on Thursday ordered four Iranian diplomats to leave the country and the European Union (EU) invited member countries to recall their ambassadors from Tehran for consultations about the future of relations with Iran.
In response, Iran withdrew its ambassador from Germany and expelled four German diplomats.
Analysts said that while the dispute was not likely to have an immediate impact on oil supply from Iran, it could force the EU to drop its opposition to U.S. trade sanctions against Tehran.
Iran, a member of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), is the world's third largest oil exporter after Saudi Arabia and Norway.
The analysts said attempts to improve relations between Iran and its oil-rich Gulf neighbours could also suffer, they said.

London-based brokers GNI, commenting on the Iran-Germany dispute, said in their daily energy report on Friday: "This is a notable development because if the move goes as far as economic sanctions, the oil industry could be affected.
"However, considering the vested interests of some oil importers within the (European) Union, we do not expect any sustainable or even workable agreement as far as energy policy is concerned".
The European Union has in the past refused to join U.S. trade sanctions against Iran and has attacked U.S. legislation providing for measures against firms that invest in its oil or gas industry.

Washington welcomed the German court ruling as a victory for its efforts to persuade Germany to take a tougher line with Tehran, which it accuses of state terrorism, and it called on the EU to adopt sanctions.

Brokers also said that the oil market firmed on news that temperatures were below normal on Friday in the U.S. northeast, the world's largest heating oil market. The weather forecast for Sunday to Tuesday showed temperatures would be below normal up to Monday and possibly Tuesday.
"With the weather in the U.S. lifting heating oil demand and gasoline offtake still to reach peak levels, the short-term fundamental outlook has improved a little," brokers GNI said in its report.

However, oil prices remain under pressure from rising Iraqi exports under the U.N. oil-for-food deal, with Iraqi crude sales now thought to be running at some 800,000 barrels a day (bpd), up from just over 500,000 bpd early in the year.

The extra sales are needed for Baghdad to meet a permitted $2 billion target by the end of June. U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan said he expected the Security Council to renew the oil-for-food deal with Iraq when it expires in June.
